pr_body:
Currently both AttributeSet/Map are immutable requiring building to
 happen (in case of Map) through a dedicated builder.
We have a number of rules where this forces creation of a lot of clones
 due to constant addition, across nodes (and thus not in one place) of
 more attributes.

The combine/intersect/disjunct methods remain as is and return new
 instances however add/remove/removeIf methods should be properly
 implemented.
This will keep the existing code working while allowing a different
 pattern - that in which the backing collection is modified up to date.

Fix #98482
pr_comments:
> LGTM and I have no comment code wise.
> 
> It is a fundamental change in approaching these collections and, while it makes perfect sense to want to have less instances created/garbage collected, why wasn't this code like this from the start? What was the original intention with this Map and Set to be implemented that way (always returning a new collection on every operation)?

To avoid cases where the outputSet of a plan ends up being modified. That is being defensive around returned collections which is an outlier since everywhere else (properties/expressions()) that is not the case. Our code should not be defensive.

Regarding why now? There were not any many rules (I think just one) that had to work on the Map. In fact many times I debated whether these collections actually are useful since in plenty of places we use just a `LinkedHashMap`. The type of queries in ESQL end up being different than those we support in ES SQL - we don't care just about combine/etc but also about the content of the original map.

issue_context.title: Security privileges for ESQL Enrich
issue_context.body:
Filing this issue to track a question/comment that was raised by @ywangd  here https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/98309#discussion_r1294115440

One question I do have is why we chose to [execute the LookupRequest with the enrich origin](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/2e4440ff1c0decf79f8a40688566411f7d518aa7/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/enrich/EnrichLookupService.java#L141C2-L141C2). It means the following query works when the user has access to only the playlist index without access to either the songs enrich policy or its associated index.

```
FROM playlist | ENRICH songs ON song_id
```

It feels a bit weird to me that we have no control on who can use what enrich process. That said, we don't have a good story around enrich and ingest pipeline either, i.e. we have no control over who can use what pipeline where a pipeline can contain an enrich processor. There have been quite a few complaints from users and we have an https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/57586 for it. I wonder whether we should not repeat the problem here with ES|QL. On the surface, it might be easier to tackle compared to ingest pipelines since ES|QL is read-only and has no "bulk" operations. What do you think?
comments:
Reposting Nhat's comment from https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/98309#discussion_r1295011961 to keep discussion in one place

---
The primary reason we perform the enrich lookup with the enrich origin is to prevent the warning that arises when accessing enrich indices, which are system indices. An alternative is to override allowSystemIndexAccessByDefault in the rest layer, but I felt that it might be too broad. I'm happy to iterate on it.
@costin This issue got closed by #98641. But I don't see how the two are related. I guess it was an accident? Should I re-open this issue?

review_comments:
question/suggestion: doesn't this potentially lead to lots of specialcasing wherever client code needs to add something to an `AttributeMap`? Technically, I'd need to check whether I have the empty attribute map whenever I call `AttributeMap::add`, no? Also, seems like conceptually the empty map has a different contract than a general attribute map.

IMHO it'd be better to have `emptyAttributeMap` return a freshly-made empty map, then all attribute maps would be consistently mutable.

It follow the convention of Java collections.  The client can create an empty collection which is mutable - however for the common case where an immutable empty collection is used, there's emptyAttributeMap similar to Collections.emptyMap()/Set()/empty().
The whole promise of the method is to return a constant - the same old empty map; which needs to be immutable since otherwise it gets modified and thus all the other places where it is being used now contain non-empty maps.
Ah, thanks for clarifying - I was unaware of the convention.
